documents.title: VigiBase WHO global database of individual case safety reports

chunks.content: Key Points Introduction Cytokines play a central role in the development and treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, with many signaling through the Janus kinase/signal transducers and activators of transcription (JAK/STAT) pathway [ ]. JAK inhibitors are indicated for a variety of inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, with approvals for diseases such as spondyloarthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, atopic dermatitis and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) [ , ]. RA as a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease affects 1% of the global population [ ]. Patients with RA exhibit osteoporosis as a frequent co-morbidity, which increases the risk of bone fractures [ ]. Osteoporosis and fractures lead to a significant reduction in functional impairment and a decreased quality of life for patients [ , ]. The initial treatment involves glucocorticoids and non-steroid anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), followed by synthetic disease modifying drugs (sDMARDs) and biologic disease modifying drugs (bDMARDs) as secondary options [ , ]. Especially glucocorticoids and NSAIDs have shown associations with increased fracture risks in this already vulnerable population [ , ]. JAK inhibitors specifically target the JAK/STAT pathway by inhibiting one or more intracellular tyrosine kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2) and block cytokine signalling [ , ]. Tofacitinib was the first substance in class approved for the treatment of RA by the US Food and Drug Association (FDAs) in 2012. Other JAK inhibitors were approved by FDA/European Medicines Agency (EMA) for RA [ ]. The JAK inhibitor abrocitinib was recently approved for atopic dermatitis, but not for the treatment of RA [ ]. While the primary pharmacological action of JAK inhibitors involves cytokine-signalling inhibition, recent studies have shown additional effects. Tofacitinib and baricitinib exhibit direct positive effects on bone synthesis and osteoblast function in murine models, without directly affecting osteoclasts [ ]. The European Medicines Agency endorsed a recent update to the summary of product characteristics (SmPC) for tofacitinib, introducing a warning about an increased fracture risk [ , ]. In September 2022 the SmPC for tofacitinib was updated to include this new adverse drug reaction [ ]. Due to the paucity of data and clinical studies with controversial outcomes [ – ], the objective of the current study was to analyze the real-world reports on bone fractures in association with the JAK inhibitors tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib and abrocitinib, which were previously assessed in an EMA referral on an increased risk of cancer and major cardiovascular events [ ]. This study was designed to assess time-trends of reports, patient demographics, and disproportionality of fracture for approved JAK inhibitors to assess a potential class effect and contribute to gain insights on the ongoing discussion on the safety profile of JAK inhibitors in clinical practice. Methods Data Source Pharmacovigilance data were obtained from VigiBase, the WHO database of adverse drug reactions reporting, which is managed by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC) [ , ]. Since 1968, VigiBase has collected and processed worldwide adverse drug reactions (ADRs). These ADRs are reported as individual case safety reports (ICSRs) by more than 140 countries. Over 30 million reports have been obtained from healthcare professionals, patients and pharmaceutical companies. The ICSRs contain information about sex, age, country, reactions and medications that can be associated with the reported ADR. The reports vary in completeness, and the likelihood of establishing a causal association is not uniform across all entries. All potential ADRs within VigiBase are documented and categorized using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA ® ) version 25.1. Data Extraction and Outcomes This study included ICSRs reporting active ingredients of tofacitinib, upadacitinib, baricitinib, filgotinib and abrocitinib as suspect or interacting drugs focusing on JAK inhibitors for chronic inflammatory disorders that were included in the EMA referral in October 2022. The data extraction was with the dataset date of on 14 March 2023. The comparator group for disproportionality were all other reports in VigiBase during the same period as the JAK inhibitors. The primary outcome of interest in this study was reporting of bone fractures. Bone fractures were identified by the MedDRA ® High-Level Group Term (MedDRA ® HLGT) “Fracture”. Avulsion fractures and tooth fractures were omitted from the analysis, as they were not classified as typical bone fractures. The full list of fractures identified in the analysis is listed in supplementary table . Data Analysis The demographics of the ICSRs were tabulated using counts and proportions or means and standard deviations (SD) for each individual JAK inhibitor. The ICSRs were stratified by the JAK inhibitor active ingredient and the primary outcome (bone fracture). ICSRs listing more than one JAK inhibitor as suspect or interacting were treated as separate reports. Co-medications were grouped and identified in the VigiBase database. Data Analysis The demographics of the ICSRs were tabulated using counts and proportions or means and standard deviations (SD) for each individual JAK inhibitor. The ICSRs were stratified by the JAK inhibitor active ingredient and the primary outcome (bone fracture). ICSRs listing more than one JAK inhibitor as suspect or interacting were treated as separate reports. Co-medications were grouped and identified in the VigiBase database. ICSRs with more than one of the same comedication group was counted as a single entry. ICSRs with a recorded age equal to 0 months and without any other hint of transplacental administration were set to age “unknown”. A disproportionality analysis was conducted using the ROR along with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) [ ]. The RORs were calculated for each individual JAK inhibitor as well as for the overall reports within VigiBase. This disproportionality method aims to compare the observed versus the expected reporting ratio for an specific event and a medicinal product [ ]. Disproportionality analyses were performed to examine the outcome of interest, and the expected reporting ratio was determined by considering the ICSRs of all medications in VigiBase, except the ones under investigation. In a secondary analysis, we examined age and gender as potential confounders. Disproportionality was assessed for females and males, and ROR was calculated for adults aged ≥ 75 years. To address confounding, we used TNF-alpha inhibitors (ATC code L04AB tumor necrosis factor alpha [TNF- alpha] inhibitors) as an alternative comparator group and repeated the disproportionality analyses. We complied to the READUS-PV guidelines on the reporting of a disproportionality analysis for drug safety signal detection using individual case safety reports in pharmacovigilance [ ]. A time series analysis was conducted for all reports of each JAK inhibitor as well as for the overall reporting covering the period from the first quarter of 2014 to the first quarter of 2023. The analyses included both fracture-specific ICSRs and overall ICSRs. The cut-off date for the analysis was set at 13 September 2022, marking the date of the EMA updated the tofacitinib SmPC. This cut-off line was employed to delineate a distinct period in the analysis corresponding to the regulatory update. All analyses were executed using the statistical software R (version 4.2.2), ensuring a robust and standardized approach to the examination of the temporal patterns in reported fracture cases associated with JAK inhibitors. This time series analysis serves to elucidate trends, potential fluctuations, and noteworthy patterns in the reporting frequency of fractures over the specified period. Results Demographics Table provides a comprehensive overview of the demographic characteristics extracted from 165,619 ICSRs overall and stratified by the five JAK inhibitors: tofacitinib ( n = 122,037), upadacitinib ( n = 27,786), bariticinib ( n = 14,616), filgotinib (830) and abrocitinib ( n = 350). Overall, female patients accounted for the majority of patients (76.2%) and the mean age was 59.1 years (SD 13.9). Most of the reports originated from North America (77.3%) followed by Europe (14.5%). The reporting peak was observed in 2022 (21.8%) succeeded by 2021 (15.9%) and 2019 (15.4%). RA was the predominant reported indication (51.9%), with the exception of abrocitinib reports. The most frequently overall reported comedication of interest for all ICSRs was sDMARDS (14.9%), followed by NSAIDs (7.8%) and glucocorticoids (7.1%). A list of the specific comedication can be found in Supplementary Table . The mean number of medications per patient was 2.4 (SD 3.3) and most patients reported using 0–4 total number of medications (87.1%). Among all ICSRs, 2987 (1.8%) documented bone fracture as an ADR, with tofacitinib having 2198 (1.8%), upadacitinib 634 (2.3%), baricitinib 144 (1.0%), filgotinib 10 (1.2%) and abrocitinib 1 (0.3%), respectively (Table ). A range of 38 different bone fractures were reported, with hip fractures (12.3%), upper limp fractures (10.7%) and lower limb fractures (8.8%) being the most frequently documented (Supplementary Table 1). ICSRs with bone fractures reported as an ADR showed a higher proportion of female gender (87.8% versus 76.2%) older average age (66.3 versus 59.1 years), compared with the patients without reported fracture, respectively. Elderly patients (> 65 years) were more common in the fracture reports (49.5%) compared with overall reports (29.1%). Comedication usage was higher in patients with fractures than without (mean 3.6 versus 2.4 drugs), while sDMARDs (23.4%), NSAIDs (13.8%) and glucocorticoids (12.6%) were the most frequently reported drug classes. These trends were consistent across all JAK inhibitors. Disproportionate Analysis Figure illustrates the result of the disproportionate analysis (also Supplementary Table ). The overall ROR for all JAK inhibitors was 3.35 (95% CI 3.23–3.48) with a similar ROR being observed for tofacitinib (3.34, 95% CI 3.20–3.48). These trends were consistent across all JAK inhibitors. Disproportionate Analysis Figure illustrates the result of the disproportionate analysis (also Supplementary Table ). The overall ROR for all JAK inhibitors was 3.35 (95% CI 3.23–3.48) with a similar ROR being observed for tofacitinib (3.34, 95% CI 3.20–3.48). Upadacitinib exhibited the highest ROR of 4.23 (95% CI 3.80–4.57), while baricitinib demonstrated the lowest ROR of 1.80 (95% CI 1.52–2.11). The ROR for filgotinib was 2.24 (95% CI 1.11–3.94). Abrocitinib had one bone fracture reported and no disproportionate analysis was conducted due to the low reporting. All the calculated RORs were statistically significant and had p values below 0.05. In patients with baricitinib, the proportion of those using NSAID or corticosteroid was similar between those with fractures and those without fractures. In secondary analyses focusing on age and gender (Supplementary Table ), significant results were consistent except for males in the baricitinib group. When TNF-alpha inhibitors were used as a comparator group, the overall ROR was also constistent; ROR 1.87 (1.80–1.95). Time Series Analysis Figure a and b illustrate the reporting trend over time, highlighting the SmPC update of tofacitinib as a vertical line. Figure a shows the overall reporting of cases related to JAK inhibitor use and Fig. b shows the reporting of fracture-related cases. Abrocitinib was not included in Fig. a and b due to low reporting. The time series analysis showed an increase in total and fracture-related reports especially for upadacitinib. The total reports for upadacitinib increased from 13,467 to 27,786 in 2022 Q3 to 2023 Q1 and reporting of fractures increased from 387 to 634 in the same period. For all JAK inhibitors, the total reporting and fractures-related reports increased after the tofacitinib SmPC update driven by tofacitinib and upadacitinib reports. For tofacitinib, a small increase in total ICSRs reported was observed; however, the reporting of ICSRs mentioning bone fractures did not increase after the SmPC update. No notable changes in reporting patterns were found for baricitinib and filgotinib after the update. The results from the full dataset used for the time series analysis are displayed in supplementary table . Discussion The findings of this real-world pharmacovigilance study elucidate a significant association between use of JAK-inhibitors and an increased reporting of bone fractures. Notably, the disproportionality analyses demonstrated elevated ROR with a safety signal for upadacitinib, tofacitinib and filgotinib, indicating a potential risk of bone fractures compared to other medications. The predominance of female patients and the higher average age in patients with fractures align with established osteoporosis risk factors. Co-medication usage, particularly with NSAIDs and glucocorticoids, is noteworthy in patients with reported fractures. The results support existing warnings for tofacitinib and raise concerns for other JAK inhibitors such as upadactinib, baricitinib and filgotinib. However, until now, a regulatory update has only been issued for tofacitinib so far. Among the JAK inhibitors, upadacitinib demonstrated the highest ROR; however, with limited existing real-world evidence for the other JAK inhibitors a potential class effect for JAK inhibitors cannot be ruled out based on the observed disproportionality. JAK inhibitors with selectivity for JAK1 and JAK2 can impede osteoclastogenesis by suppressing receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa beta (RANKL) expression [ ]. A small clinical study demonstrated that one year of treatment with tofacitinib led to a statistically significant increase in bone mineral density at the lumbar spine (4.6%, 95% CI 3.8–5.4%) and femoral neck (3.0%, 95% CI 2.2–3.8%), as well as a decrease in bone resorption markers [ ]. This indicates that the JAK inhibitors could have a positive effect on bone metabolism. The broad range of pharmacological effects, particularly affecting bone metabolism and the immune system, have raised new concerns about potential long-term adverse effects on bone metabolism, which may contribute to an increased incidence of bone fractures [ ]. These concerns and conflicting data have resulted in the SmPC for tofacitinib to be updated in September 2022 [ , ]. However, studies using bone fracture as the primary outcome are limited in literature and clinical evidence is sparse. A post-authorization study, using the WHO global pharmacovigilance database (VigiBase), presented secondary findings regarding the incidence rates of fractures for tofacitinib and baricitinib [ ]. The reported information component (IC 025 ) values were 1.6 for tofacitinib and 0.4 for baricitinib [ ]. A Korean study using spontaneous reports and online patient reviews found an overall reporting odds ratio (ROR) of 1.49 (95% CI 1.03–2.14) for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib [ ]. However, these findings were secondary and not a specific focus in the articles [ , ]. The results obtained from our study comply with results from these published real-world studies, although they did not

The reported information component (IC 025 ) values were 1.6 for tofacitinib and 0.4 for baricitinib [ ]. A Korean study using spontaneous reports and online patient reviews found an overall reporting odds ratio (ROR) of 1.49 (95% CI 1.03–2.14) for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib [ ]. However, these findings were secondary and not a specific focus in the articles [ , ]. The results obtained from our study comply with results from these published real-world studies, although they did not focus on fractures as an adverse event related to JAK inhibitor use and potential risk factors for bone fractures [ , ]. The study by Hoisnard et al. used data from 126,815 ICSRs associated with JAK inhibitors and found a 1.7% occurrence of fractures, which closely aligns with our findings of 1.8% [ ]. In the study by Hoisnard et al., tofacitinib exhibited a higher IC 025 compared with baricitinib, a trend that our disproportionate analysis also supports. The Korean study using spontaneous reports and online patient reviews from the USA and Korea, reported an odds ratio of 1.49 (95% CI 1.03–2.14) for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib, which is lower than our findings [ ]. This disparity in results can be attributed to the differences in data collection sources. Patient reviews, while valuable, can vary in terms of accuracy, completeness and reliability [ ]. Findings from these two real-world studies consistently demonstrated a potential class effect for JAK inhibitors on bone fractures, which aligns with the findings of our current study. In 2022, the EMA and Swissmedic issued recommendations to minimize serious side effects associated with Janus kinase inhibitors, including thromboembolism, malignancy and infections [ , ]. The ORAL Surveillance study indicated higher risks of cancer and major cardiovascular events with tofacitinib. The increased fracture risk also refers to this study, although these results are not included in the published trial. The significance of considering risk factors in the latest SmPC update for tofacitinib advises cautious use in patients with known factors predisposing to fractures, including elderly individuals, females and those undergoing corticosteroid therapy, irrespective of indication and dosage [ ]. The EMA and Swissmedic are regulatory bodies that issued a safety warning regarding bone fractures associated with use of the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib. While the warning specifically applies to tofacitinib, our results indicate potential association of bone fractures for other JAK inhibitors with a potential class effect. The duration of drug exposure may affect the risk of fractures, such as the development of osteoporosis. This might also be reflected in the length of market use among different substances within the JAK inhibitor class, with tofacitinib being the oldest. Future studies should also consider including newer JAK inhibitors such as decernotinib, peficitinib, itacitinib, delgocitinib and gusacitinib to provide a more comprehensive understanding of this class of drugs. Another observation was the higher ROR for upadacitinib compared with other JAK inhibitors. Upadacitinib and filgotinib are JAK1 selective inhibitors, while tofacitinib is non-specific and baricitinib is selective for JAK1 and JAK2 [ ]. An in vitro study concluded that inhibition of JAK1/2 receptors suppressed RANKL-expression and inhibited development of osteoclast, leading a decrease in bone desorption [ ]. In vivo data from knockout mice with inflammatory bone destruction showed that treatment with the JAK1-speific inhibitor, ABT-318, blocked bone destruction by targeting mature osteoclasts [ ]. Findings from in vivo/in vitro experiments indicate a preventive effect on bone destruction; however, our findings are not in line with the experimental data. A hypothesis for the occurrence of bone fractures associated with JAK inhibitor use is the inhibition of cytokines. Cytokines and interleukins (ILs), such as IL-3, IL-6 and IL-17, have a key role in maintaining bone formation and upregulates osteoblast genesis, leading to an increase in bone formation [ – ]. These cytokines are regulated by JAK1/JAK2 receptors and inhibition will result in production of less cytokines. This could potentially disturb the bone remodeling balance and lead to increased bone resorption. Inhibition of JAK receptors will have extensive effects on bone metabolism and cytokine signaling, which can lead to an increased fracture risk. However, more studies are needed to confirm the effect of JAK selectivity and cytokine inhibition on bone fracture risks. In secondary analyses using TNF-alpha inhibitors as a comparator group, both tofacitibin and upadacitinib were associated with increased reporting of fractures (ROR 1.82, 95% CI 1.74–1.91 for tofacitinib and 2.23, 95%CI: 2.06–2.42 for upadacitinib). This analysis suggests that the increased reporting of fractures with these drugs may not be solely attributed to comedication use, but rather to other factors such as drug-specific or class effects. In secondary analyses using TNF-alpha inhibitors as a comparator group, both tofacitibin and upadacitinib were associated with increased reporting of fractures (ROR 1.82, 95% CI 1.74–1.91 for tofacitinib and 2.23, 95%CI: 2.06–2.42 for upadacitinib). This analysis suggests that the increased reporting of fractures with these drugs may not be solely attributed to comedication use, but rather to other factors such as drug-specific or class effects. Our results indicate increased reporting of bone fractures globally for tofacitinib, upadacitinib and baricitinib, suggesting a potential class effect. The potential mechanism could be associated with cytokine signaling inhibition and direct effects on bone metabolism. Our findings propose further evaluation and potential adjustments of the SmPCs of other JAK inhibitors. Limitations The present study has certain limitations, particularly concerning the database and source of reporting. It should be noted that spontaneous reporting is not suitable for estimating the prevalence or incidence of adverse events among patients exposed to drugs [ ]. Another significant limitation is the lack of case-causality assessment. Individual case safety reports may not provide conclusive evidence of a causal association due to the absence of information on potential alternative causes and incomplete data regarding the timing of adverse events [ ]. The information comes from a variety of sources, and the probability that the suspected adverse effect is drug-related is not the same in all cases [ ]. Baricitinib was the first JAK inhibitor licensed in Europe in both the 2 mg and 4 mg formulation, but only the 2 mg formulation was approved by the FDA due to safety concerns. It is not clear, if there is a dose-dependence of the reaction, but this may explain the higher reporting rates from this region. While treatment guidelines for rheumatoid arthritis and management of comorbidities such as osteoporosis are broadly aligned between Europe and the USA, there may still be regional differences in co-medication practices, treatment duration, or dosage that could influence fracture risk [ , ]. However, due to the limitations of the current pharmacovigilance dataset, we are unable to perform a detailed analysis of these potential regional variations. ICSRs reported to VigiBase doubled for upadacitinib between 2022 Q3 and 2023 Q1, while reporting for other JAK inhibitors remained stable. This increase resulted in a surge in reported bone fractures compared to other approved JAK inhibitors. The cause for this rise is not clear, but increased regulatory communication and approval of new indications could be factors [ , ]. In 2022, the EMA and Swissmedic issued recommendations to minimize serious side effects associated with Janus kinase inhibitors, including thromboembolism, malignancy and infections [ , ]. An alert concerning a drug adverse reaction may also lead to a “ripple effect”, resulting in an increase in reports of the adverse reaction with other drugs in the same pharmacological or therapeutic class as the drug initially flagged in the alert [ ]. This phenomenon should be considered when interpreting the increased reporting of adverse reactions, as it may not be limited to a single drug but affect others within the class as well. The present work is subject to other study-specific limitations that should be acknowledged. One limitation is specific to the availability of data for filgotinib and abrocitinib. The sparse number of reported cases for these drugs constrained the ability to conduct comprehensive analyses. Furthermore, the low number of reports for abrocitinib prevented a disproportionate analysis. Another significant limitation concerns the selected outcome of interest, namely bone fractures. Unlike immediate adverse events, the occurrence of a bone fracture is a complex outcome that does not directly establish a causal link to the administered drug within the database [ ]. Bone fractures are influenced by many factors, including mechanistic stress, which may not be linked to the use of JAK inhibitors or other reported comedication [ ]. Rheumatoid arthritis is a known risk factor for fractures [ , ]. In our analysis, we observed a higher proportion of patients with RA among those using upadacitinib compared with tofacitinib. This difference in the proportion of patients with RA may contribute to the observed variation in fracture risk. We acknowledge that this factor could influence our findings, and we recommend conducting sensitivity analyses in future studies to account for the impact of RA and other relevant variables. The risk of fracture is increased with long-term use of drugs such as oral glucocorticoids or NSAIDs. Due to limitations in data availability and technical constraints, we could not adjust for concurrent medication or specific indications. Nevertheless, using TNF-alpha inhibitors as a comparator yielded comparable results (ROR 1.87, 95% CI 1.80–1.95). The risk of fracture is increased with long-term use of drugs such as oral glucocorticoids or NSAIDs. Due to limitations in data availability and technical constraints, we could not adjust for concurrent medication or specific indications. Nevertheless, using TNF-alpha inhibitors as a comparator yielded comparable results (ROR 1.87, 95% CI 1.80–1.95). Future studies with real-world data should further investigate the impact of co-medication and indication on fracture risk in patients using JAK inhibitors. Despite these limitations, our analysis adjusted for other potential confounding factors such as age and gender, were consistent with the primary findings. It is important to interpret the findings of this study considering these limitations, as they affect the generalizability and conclusive determination of causality. Despite these limitations, the utilization of pharmacovigilance analyses, such as disproportionality analysis, remains a valuable method for identifying safety signals. The extensive global coverage of VigiBase, encompassing data from more than 140 countries, enhances the detection of adverse events related to JAK inhibitors [ ]. Pharmacovigilance data can support decision making for regulatory authorities and the utilization of spontaneous reporting is an effective approach for monitoring the safety profile of medications throughout their lifespan. Conclusion Results obtained from this real-world pharmacovigilance study add to the ongoing clinical and regulatory debate regarding the safety profile of JAK inhibitors. Patients with a bone fracture were mostly female, elderly and frequently reported use of medications associated with risks of bone fractures, such as glucocorticoids. Fracture reports have increased for tofacitinib, upadacitinib, baricitinib and filgotinib, suggesting a potential class effect on bone fracture among JAK inhibitors. However, cautious interpretation is required due to the nature of the data, which is subject to several limitations and biases. The association of fractures with older and female patients and concurrent medications may indicate an existing fracture risk. Although a safety update has been issued for tofacitinib in the European Union, our findings suggest the reassessment for warnings regarding other JAK inhibitors. Real-world data specific to JAK inhibitors and bone fractures is scarce, highlighting the importance of further assessment to establish a conclusive causal relationship, particularly for filgotinib and abrocitinib, where additional data is required to evaluate their impact on bone fractures.
